PASSO 1: «si» (sem acento) é o nosso «se: STEP 1: «si» (no accent) is English "if". Good news: Spanish «si» sentences work almost exactly like the English first, second and third conditionals. The tense tells you how likely the condition is. STEP 2: there are three situations. (a) Possible: «Si tengo tiempo, voy» = "If I have time, I'll go" (session 2). (b) Unlikely or unreal now: «Si tuviera tiempo, iría» = "If I had time, I would go". (c) Impossible, in the past: «Si hubiera tenido tiempo, habría ido» = "If I had had time, I would have gone" (session 3). STEP 3: this session covers (b). English puts the "if" part in the past ("if I HAD"); Spanish puts it in the imperfecto de subjuntivo (lesson 46): «si tuviera», «si fuera», «si pudiera». STEP 4: the other part takes the simple conditional, English "would": infinitive + ía, ías, ía, íamos, íais, ían. «Viajaría, viajarías, viajaría, viajaríamos, viajaríais, viajarían.» STEP 5: some conditionals are irregular, with the same stem as the future: tendría, haría, diría, pondría, podría, querría, vendría, saldría, sabría, habría, valdría. STEP 6: never put the conditional in the «si» part — just as careful English avoids "if I would have money". «Si tendría dinero» is wrong; you may hear it in some regions, but standard Spanish avoids it. STEP 7: the two parts can swap places: «Viajaría más si tuviera dinero» = «Si tuviera dinero, viajaría más». If the «si» part comes first, use a comma. STEP 8: to give advice, use «Yo, en tu lugar, + conditional» or «Si yo fuera tú, + conditional» — English "If I were you…": «Si yo fuera tú, hablaría con él». The "were" is «fuera», never «era».
o português tem a mesma estrutura: «Se e: English conditionals map neatly: "If I had money, I'd travel" = «Si tuviera dinero, viajaría»; "If I were you" = «Si yo fuera tú». Where English uses the past after "if", Spanish uses the past subjunctive; where English uses "would", Spanish uses the conditional. And the rule you already follow in English — no "would" after "if" — is strict in Spanish: never «si tendría».

PASSO 1: para uma condição possível no p: STEP 1: for a possible condition in the present or future, the «si» part takes the present indicative, and the other part the present, future or imperative — exactly like the English first conditional: «Si llueve, me quedo en casa», «Si llueve, me quedaré en casa» (If it rains, I'll stay home), «Si llueve, quédate en casa». STEP 2: never use the present subjunctive or the future after «si» in a condition: not «si llueva», not «si lloverá». (Exception: when «si» means "whether" in an indirect question: «No sé si lloverá» — I don't know whether it'll rain.) STEP 3: «si no» means "if not": «Si no estudias, no aprobarás». It's two words; «sino» (one word) means "but rather" (lesson 52). STEP 4: for past habits, use the imperfecto de indicativo in both parts: «Si hacía frío, nos quedábamos en casa» (If it was cold, we stayed / used to stay home). Here «si» means "whenever". STEP 5: a shorter, more formal form uses «de» + infinitive instead of the «si» part: «De tener dinero, viajaría» = «Si tuviera dinero, viajaría»; «De haberlo sabido, te habría avisado» (Had I known, I would have told you). You'll find it in writing. STEP 6: «si» also introduces indirect questions ("whether"): «No sé si viene». It never takes the subjunctive there. STEP 7: «por si acaso» and «por si» + indicative express precaution, English "in case": «Llévate el paraguas por si llueve» (Take the umbrella in case it rains). STEP 8: in polite requests, «si pudiera…» softens the request: «Si pudiera ayudarme con esto, se lo agradecería» (If you could help me with this, I'd be grateful). Combine the «si» part with the conditional.

PASSO 1: para falar do que não aconteceu: STEP 1: to talk about what didn't happen in the past — the English third conditional, "If I had studied, I would have passed" — you need two pieces. STEP 2: the first piece is the pluscuamperfecto de subjuntivo, English "had + past participle" in the «si» part. It's formed with the imperfecto de subjuntivo of «haber» (hubiera, hubieras, hubiera, hubiéramos, hubierais, hubieran) plus the participle: «hubiera estudiado», «hubiera comido». The -se set also exists: «hubiese estudiado». STEP 3: the second piece is the condicional compuesto (lesson 41), English "would have": «habría» + participle, as in «habría aprobado». STEP 4: put them together: «Si hubiera estudiado, habría aprobado» (I didn't study, I didn't pass). In speech, the main part can also use «hubiera» instead of «habría»: «Si hubiera estudiado, hubiera aprobado». Both are accepted. STEP 5: the most famous English-speaker mistake is the colloquial "if I would have known": in Spanish that becomes «si habría sabido», which is wrong. The «si» part is always «hubiera»: «Si lo hubiera sabido». STEP 6: the irregular participles are the same ones you use in the pretérito perfecto: hecho, dicho, puesto, visto, escrito, vuelto, abierto, roto, muerto, cubierto. STEP 7: you can mix past and present, like an English mixed conditional: «Si hubiera aceptado ese trabajo, ahora viviría en Barcelona» (If I had taken that job, I would be living in Barcelona now). STEP 8: regrets use «ojalá» + pluscuamperfecto — English "I wish I had": «Ojalá hubiera estudiado más». Unreal comparisons in the past use «como si» + pluscuamperfecto: «Me miró como si no me hubiera visto nunca» (as if he had never seen me).
